business.overview:
Allarity has no commercial drug revenue. Its core asset is stenoparib, an oral inhibitor of PARP1/2 and tankyrase 1/2, paired with a gene-expression-based Drug Response Predictor intended to select patients more likely to benefit. The lead program is Phase 2 ovarian cancer; a VA-funded Phase 2 combination trial targets relapsed small-cell lung cancer.

The transmission channel is clinical, not macroeconomic: stronger prospective evidence that DRP scores identify responders could improve the probability and design of a registrational study. CLIA certification brings testing in-house, while the API campaign supplies late-stage-quality drug material. Neither milestone substitutes for controlled efficacy, safety or regulatory agreement.

The equity case breaks if enrollment stalls, DRP-selected patients do not show reproducible benefit, FDA requirements expand, or financing occurs faster than clinical de-risking. With no product revenue, shareholder value is highly sensitive to cash runway, Tumim purchase-facility usage, warrant exercises, debt service and the terms of any partner or capital raise.
business.moat: The only credible moat is the combination of exclusive stenoparib rights, drug-specific DRP know-how, a CLIA-certified testing workflow and patent protection for stenoparib-plus-DRP patient selection into April 2042. It remains a prospective moat: clinical validation and regulatory acceptance are required before it has durable economic value.

The AI and defense transmission channel runs through orbital and lunar data infrastructure: spacecraft collect information, ground stations move it, and mission systems process it for civil, commercial and national-security customers. The Goonhilly and COMSAT acquisition broadens coverage, while NSNS investment targets recurring network revenue rather than one-off lander missions.

The model breaks when awards fail to convert into profitable milestones. business.overview:
Sterling operates through E-Infrastructure, Transportation and Building Solutions. E-Infrastructure performs site development and electrical work for data centers, manufacturing and semiconductor facilities; Transportation builds public roads and related assets; Building supplies concrete and plumbing work to housing and commercial projects.

The AI transmission channel is physical: hyperscaler and enterprise compute spending becomes data-center land preparation, utilities and mission-critical electrical work. CEC expanded Sterling from site development into electrical services, increasing the amount of each project the company can capture. At Q2, mission-critical work represented 92% of E-Infrastructure backlog and carried the growth profile.

The model breaks if data-center awards are delayed, acquired businesses miss margin targets, unsigned awards fail to convert, or fixed-price labor and material costs outrun estimates. Housing affordability is already pressuring Building, while Sterling is deliberately shifting resources away from lower-growth Transportation projects toward higher-margin E-Infrastructure assignments.
business.moat: Sterling's moat is execution capacity in complex site-development and electrical packages, regional operating density, customer relationships and a safety/selection discipline that favors higher-margin work. CEC broadens the service stack, but the moat depends on maintaining project-level margins while integrating acquisitions and scaling labor.
